Q: Trouble with well-foundedness proofs A:

Acc_C2 recurses on the given Acc ltA a proof. Revert y before the induction because in the ltF_C2_C2 predecessor case the Y component is not fixed: the constructor has both y1 and y2.

coq
Lemma Acc_C2 : forall y : Y, forall a : A, Acc ltA a -> Acc ltF (C2 y a).
Proof.
  intros y a Ha.
  revert y.
  induction Ha as [a Ha IHa].
  intro y.
  constructor.
  intros f Hf.
  inversion Hf; subst.
  - apply Acc_C1.
  - eapply IHa; eassumption.
Qed.

Theorem wf_ltF : well_founded ltF.
Proof.
  intro f.
  destruct f as [x | y a].
  - apply Acc_C1.
  - apply Acc_C2.
    apply wf_ltA.
Qed.

In the C2/C2 case, after inverting Hf : ltF f (C2 y a), the predecessor has the form C2 y1 a1 with ltA a1 a. The induction hypothesis from Acc ltA a provides accessibility for a1, and because y was reverted first, it works for any y1.

The C1 predecessor case does not recurse through ltA; it is closed directly by Acc_C1.

Q: JUnit assertEquals( ) fails for two objects, but `equals()` returns true A:

You haven't actually overridden equals - you've overloaded it instead. Use the @Override annotation to find this sort of thing out at compile time.

In other words, you've got:

public boolean equals(MyClass other)

where you should have:

@Override // Force the compiler to check I'm really overriding something
public boolean equals(Object other)

In your working assertion, you were calling the overloaded method as the compile-time type of obj1 and obj2 were both MyClass. JUnit's assertEquals will only call equals(Object) as it doesn't know any better.

Q: How to increase maximum Docker Network on one server? A:

Docker’s default bridge pools are exhausted because the default configuration creates a limited number of /16 (172.x) and /20 (192.168.x) networks.

Changing

{
  "base": "172.16.0.0/12",
  "size": 24
}

does not increase the total address space.

It simply partitions the same /12 private range into many more /24 networks (4096 instead of only 16 /16 networks), which is usually a much better trade-off for Docker Compose projects.

This becomes very visible when running many Compose projects or Docker-in-Docker environments. I hit the default limit after about 20 bridge networks even though almost none of the address space was actually used.

Q: Is this possible to customize printf? A:

Most answers have one of two major disadvantages:

  • They give up on the beauty and brevity of printf, or
  • They give up on the de-facto type-safety that real-world compilers use to check the format string against the argument types actually passed.

However, with C11 (or GNU C compiler extensions if you live in the dark ages - note that this is completely unrelated to the GNU C library extensions mentioned in some other answers), it is possible to avoid both problems.

A sketch of a solution:

  • Define a type memory_pool along with (at least) 2 operations:

    • allocate an object (usually, a string)
    • free all objects in the pool

  • Define a function-like macro convert_for_printf that uses _Generic to convert each possible type (usually, to a char * owned by the pool, though nothing requires this, it only has to match what the format string expects); a memory_pool object is passed since that may be needed:

    Due to the braindead specification of _Generic, all branches must be valid even if statically not taken. Which usually means you have to write a boilerplate function for each individual type involved (including all the primitives). This can be somewhat DRY'ed if you have a single fwd.h header that declares all types used in your program, which you can then change to use X-macros.

    If your header needs to be used from C++ you will need to write a second implementation of all this. Again, use of macros to abstract it is recommended.

  • Define a function-like macro my_printf that:

    • creates a new memory_pool
    • iterates over the variadic arguments and wraps them in convert_for_printf, then passes the format string and converted arguments to the real printf.
      • You should probably just #include <boost/preprocessor.hpp> (this one library is not C++-specific), even if its API for this is weird
    • frees the memory_pool.
    • (note that the obvious place to story the memory_pool instance implies making this a block and discarding the result of printf, which admittedly most people don't ever check; there are several approaches to solve this, but none are both universal and good since I don't think compiler will optimize away thread-local variables)

(All of this is, obviously, significantly easier if you're doing the whole thing in C++, where we can use ADL to do the dispatch, lambdas for expression-capable scopes, and destructors (perhaps in a nested function) to do the cleanup - though it turns out the cleanup is actually the easiest part here)

Q: How does ldd select which lib.so file to load? A:

How does ldd select which lib.so file to load?

There are specific rules (that also depend on specific ld.so), they are documented in man 8 ld.so. See https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/ld.so.8.html .

How to ensure that the proper library is loaded?

Use LD_PRELOAD.

Q: Deduced conflicting types for parameter const T (unsigned char and int) A:

(My) Answer from first "potential duplicates" fixes your issue:

template <class T>
const T& clamp (const T& value,
                std::type_identity_t<const T&> low,
                std::type_identity_t<const T&> high)
{
    return (value < low ? low : (value > high ? high : value));
}

Demo

T is only deduced from value. low/high will use the same T.

As you cannot change definition, you have to

  • provide same type for all arguments (cast as you do for example).
  • Specify the template explicitly: clamp<uint8_t>(other_range, range, 8);
  • provide (better) overload Demo
